2026 SEMA Show • Toyota Puts Snow Tracks on Five SUVs and Trucks, Unloads Them at SEMA 2026 as the Snowhunter Bunch
He Bought a 1976 Chevy Camaro Like He Had in High-School, but It Has No Brakes
19 photos
Photo: Royalty Auto Service | YouTube
For this guy, this is a project of nostalgia. It may not be the best car in the world, and definitely not the prettiest. Besides, it has, he says, the "worst air cleaner on the face of the planet Earth." However, he has been dreaming of buying one just like it since the moment he sold it.
Sometimes, just sometimes, nostalgia wins out, and a car guy makes emotional purchases, even though, rationally, it's a bad idea. Sherwood Cooke Jr., owner of a family-run auto repair shop in St. Marys and Kingsland, Georgia, bought a 1 976 Chevrolet Camaro very similar to the one he had when he was in high school, back in the mid-1980s.
The car was his daily driver, even though it was anything but the ideal daily driver. “It would melt your shoe on the floorboard because the headers ran right underneath the driver's side where your foot was,” he recalls.
He had bought that car from someone who had blown the engine after using water instead of coolant in a cold winter, which cracked the block, and he wasn’t going to fix it. Sherwood remembers it as if it were yesterday, but he forgot how much he paid for it. From that moment on, every paycheck he got went into that car.
Photo: Royalty Auto Service | YouTube Sure, it was far from perfect, but it brings back good memories. As for the new one, things got off on the wrong foot. He paid $12,500, even though the original asking price was $10,000. All of a sudden, the seller went straight to $25,000. Sherwood managed to negotiate it down, then load it onto the trailer and drive it to his shop.
He would have gladly driven it home on its own power, because it does run and drive, but it is not exactly drivable. It has no brakes. Sherwood's former boss and mentor, Neal, is going to save the day when it comes to the braking system and to everything else that needs work, for that matter.
He has already started ordering parts for it. He drove it around a bit and says it drives well, as the engine and transmission must have been rebuilt not too long ago. The 350 cubic-inch (5.7-liter) Small-Block V8 engine with a two-barrel carburetor setup sits under the hood.
The V8 was originally rated for a modest 165 horsepower (167 metric horsepower) and 260 pound-feet (353 Newton meters) from the Chevrolet factory. The Camaro was far from a sports car. It took nearly 10 seconds to hit 60 mph (97 kph) from a standstill and maxed out at 121 mph (195 kph).
Photo: Royalty Auto Service | YouTube However, to stop that non-sports car, he will need a new master cylinder and probably a booster. Neal will know what to do and recommends the buyer stay away from the engine. Sherwood, however, is considering new electric fans. It already has a new electric fuel pump.
The car comes with the steel bumper from the factory, a design choice that wasn’t exactly popular among Camaro enthusiasts. So the new owner is considering painting it to match the red body color. The car is finished in an orange-ish shade of red, but he is planning to change that.
" It definitely won't be pink ," he decides. Peeled paint at the base of the windshield reveals a dark red shade, which might have been the color the Camaro rolled off the production line with back in 1976, and it looks like it sported a color-coordinated cabin.
His car from back in the 1980s was finished in black and had an L88 fiberglass hood, a trend launched with the late-60s Corvette L88s, and it was a race car that he drove on the street. He wants to find a set of Cragar wheels for his new old 1976 Camaro , just like he had on his first car.
Photo: Royalty Auto Service | YouTube The doors are stuck shut, so Neil slides into the cabin through the rolled-down window, fires up the engine, and revs it up before unloading it from the trailer, hooked safely to the winch, because that is all the braking power they’ve got at this point. Back in his teenage years, he wouldn’t have minded it much.
Everything seems to work on board, except for the horn, which seems to have a mind of its own. But there are wires dangling from the upper part of the dashboard, looking like something is missing. The original radio is missing as well, but he eventually finds it wrapped in bubble wrap in the trunk.
He will also have the interior redone. His car used to have a gray interior, but this one came off the production line with seats wrapped in black vinyl. The driver’s seat shows the usual signs of wear and tear. The new owner is also planning a new shifter and aftermarket gauges that show more than the factory ones. Besides, he wants to make it look as much as possible like his old Camaro.
The newly purchased Camaro has no air conditioning, just like Sherwood’s good, old car, but it is equipped with the air cleaner that is " quite possibly the worst air cleaner on the face of the planet Earth ." But it is a love-hate situation. That is the reason he just had to buy the car.
Once he is done with the mechanical part, the new owner is going to send it to the body shop to have it repainted and repair all the dings and dents. Then, it will be the 1980s all over again.

2026 SEMA Show • 2028 Mitsubishi Outlander Diamond Trail Edition: How Does It Compare to Other Adventure Crossovers?
Best 5 Premium Hot Wheels Cars in 2026: Porsche, Ferrari and McLaren Reign Supreme
42 photos
Photo: autoevolution
Black Friday is just around the corner, and I had almost forgotten this “celebration” existed in the first place. That’s because I never take part in it, as I’ve spent enough years in the industry to realize what it’s all about. There’s only only one category of products I might be interested in.
Yes, I’m talking about diecast collectibles. Two of the biggest retailers in my area have announced discounts of up to 70% from the model’s original price. I’ll believe it when I’ll see it. I know a good price when I see one, as I spend a lot of time looking at the market.
There’s always a diecast-focused distributor who needs to go ahead with a clearance and will sell the cars for less than he paid for them in the first place. And there’s always one “enthusiast” (read scalper) that realizes he shouldn’t have gone knee deep in the “business” in the first place.
Anyway, think of that as my Sunday Hot Wheels collecting tip. The real reason I started writing this story is because I wanted to let you know what I think are the best 5 premium Hot Wheels cars in 2026.
I won’t be talking about Elite 64 and the Red Line Club for now, as there might be a few surprises left in there. Instead, I’ll be focusing on five collections that have already revealed their complete line-up to us by now.
Pop Culture: 2022 Porsche 911 GT3 RS Photo: autoevolution Now, I’ve thought about several different ways of “nominating” the Top 3 items for each category. Of course this will all be subjective, and your Top 3 can look completely different to mine. I actually encourage to let me know what your favorites are, as I’m always curious to see how Mattel’s products land with other people. Back to Pop Culture : we have seen six mixes this year, which translates to a total of 30 tiny cars.
Right off the bat, some of them don’t belong on this list as they’re repeat models from previous years. I’m talking about the Lincoln Continental from the Matrix, the Guinevere Van from Onward, the Simpsons Family Car and all the other models that aren’t even real cars. So where does that leave us? Well, if this list would have been called “The Most Hyped Cars of 2026”, the Godzilla-themed Nissan Skyline GT-R (BNR34) would have taken the win.
I’ve seen some “entrepreneurs” asking as much as $480 for these, which is downright ridiculous and offensive for a non-RLC, non-limited collectible. The 1983 BMW 733i was pretty hot, especially since it was a brand-new casting. The Forza-themed Audi 90 quattro was new to Premium, but maybe not as desirable for most.
I’d love a closer look at the James Bond -powered Lotus Esprit Turbo, and it might have won today’s “award” if it had different wheels. My vote goes to Ronald Wong’s 2022 Porsche 911 GT3 RS that pays tribute to Gran Turismo. I’m not 100% happy with the color combo, but that issue will be solved with next year’s Canyon Warriors iteration.
Boulevard: Ferrari Enzo Photo: Lamley Group The choice is a bit more complicated for the Boulevard series, despite it only having five mixes throughout the year. That adds up to 25 models, but there are no repeat ones to think of. There are also no “wacky racers”, if you know what I mean. Let’s have a quick look at the new variations for existing castings first.
The 2001 BMW M3 GTR has definitely reached new heights for its second release, and I haven’t been able to find the Metalflake Silver release anywhere in the wild. Mix 2 was a real banger, and there’s no doubt the HKS-themed Nissan Skyline GT-R (R32) Pandem was the hottest car there.
I still enjoyed the '69 Ford Torino Talladega and the Lamborghini Gallardo LP 570-4 Superleggera, and it just so happens that the latter two are the only ones I haven’t parted ways with yet. I haven’t bought a single car from Mix 3, but the nostalgic Datsun King Cab Baja Custom is my favorite there. Mix 4 was pretty big, and I’ll say it here: everyone on the planet wanted to have the Ferrari Enzo!
It’s one of eight new castings for 2026, and I even broke my own rule for it by paying 50% more than its regular retail price just so I could park it next to the F50. It was definitely a close call between the iconic supercar and the classic JDM racer!
Car Culture: Ferrari Testarossa Photo: autoevolution Car Culture further complicates the situation by featuring 48 different cars throughout the year. I will make it easier for myself here and take eight of them out of the equation right off the bat, as I’ve never even seen one of the Chase items up close. To me, it’s almost as if they don’t even exist in the first place. There’s a 5-piece set of them featuring the Datsun, Chevy, BMW , Mercedes and Nissan for sale on eBay for $1,850 if you feel otherwise.
Looking back at Japan Historics 5, it looks more enticing now than it did the first time I saw it in a toy store. I bought the least exciting one there (the Datsun 620), but I’m not sure I’d add either one of them on today’s shortlist. This might sound controversial to some of you, but the Lancia Delta S4 from Thrill Climbers is definitely going into my Top 5 for 2026.
If it had a removable hatch like you’d get on the 787B, it would have won hands down. The green BMW M3 from Power Trip was decent but not award-worthy decent. The new 1994 NISMO 270R (S14) turned out to be a peg-warmer in my area, and I’m under the impression the Porsche 993 GT2 under performed just as well.
The Ferrari Testarossa has to be a Top 3 collectible, and I’m putting it up there with the Aerostyles 2008 Audi A4 Touring Car. Vintage Racing and Road Trip haven’t provided any entries for my list, and I’m not 100% sure about Deutschland Design either. Now, I want to say the DTM-spec Audi is the winner, but I’d only do that just to avoid making this list look like a Ferrari-focused party. Do you agree the Testarossa reign supreme for Car Culture this year?
Team Transport: Team #95 (Porsche Cayenne and Porsche 944 Turbo) Photo: Lamley Group I seem to have already overextended myself here, so I’ll try to be brief moving forward. Mattel gave us four mixes of Team Transport this year for a total of 12 teams, plus the bonus Walmart Legends Tour Exclusive release.
It might be fair to go for a double award here, as each package contains two vehicles. So picking just one item doesn’t make perfect sense, but could still be a way to go about I. We only had three new castings all years.
The Mercedes-Benz 300 SLR arrived in Mix 2, Terra-Torque was a hauler in Mix 3, and the 2008 Porsche Cayenne had the same role in Mix 4. I know everyone went crazy for Team #97, as Rexy tends to get that sort of reaction from the audience.
But the new iteration of the Porsche 911 GT3 R (992) is just too similar to the First Edition of the casting to win my vote. If I had to pick just one vehicle, I would likely go for the Terra-Torque truck. However, when it comes to complete teams, #95 is the one for me as the appeal of two Porsches in one set is too strong for me to resist.
Premium Collector Sets: 1997 McLaren F1 GTR Photo: Lamley Group I initially thought about including the Car Culture 2-Packs in this list. We had four mixes there, with a total of 24 cars. Half of them were either identical or similar to previous releases, which is why I decided to “disqualify” the series from this “ceremony”.
If I had included, the Maserati MC12 would have won hands down. The Premium Collector Sets have been around for seven years now, and Mattel has gotten everyone used to seeing four packages a year. I won’t nominate the best package, as the mix inside is almost never perfect.
That means I’ll focus on the best out of 16 models instead. I think the 1957 Jeep FC from Off-Road was nice, but not amazing. The Toyota package didn’t bring anything particularly new to the table, while the Mooneyes 1934 Ford Hot Rod was pretty stunning. It just can’t compete with the Gulf-powered 1997 McLaren F1 GTR.
The hype around it was so insane, that I don’ even mind not being able to buy one for my collection. These are my favorite Premium Hot Wheels this year, I’ll be back with a look at the basic lines, Elite 64 and the Red Line Club later this month or in December the latest.

source_document.body:
Legendary truck brand Peterbilt is lowering procurement barriers for state and municipal fleets looking to electrify their assets by adding its growing lineup of medium- and heavy-duty battery electric trucks to its cooperative purchasing Agreement with Sourcewell.
The expanded purchasing contract, extended through July 2028, provides Sourcewell’s more than 50,000 member organizations access to competitively solicited contracts with pre-negotiated pricing and terms across the Peterbilt brand’s full lineup of Class 5- 8 commercial trucks . That contract allows eligible agencies to streamline procurement by sourcing Peterbilt’s on-highway, vocational and medium-duty BEVs through Sourcewell’s pre-negotiated agreement, potentially eliminating the need to go through a long, agonizing bidding process of their own.
“Our long-standing relationship with Sourcewell reflects Peterbilt’s commitment to delivering solutions tailored to the unique needs of public fleets,” explains Erik Johnson, assistant general manager of sales and marketing at Peterbilt . “By adding our electric vehicles to the contract and eliminating lengthy bidding processes, we’re helping organizations maximize uptime and invest their resources where it matters most, keeping their communities running.”
ELI5; what is Sourcewell?
PACCAR Kenworth T880E.
I hear some of you asking, “Why is this important, and what exactly is Sourcewell?” And you’re very smart to ask.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
See, when your state or local government decides it needs a new truck, it can’t just call up someone’s cousin and cut an inflated check backed by your tax dollars ( regardless of what you saw on Fox News ). Instead, public agencies generally have to follow competitive purchasing rules that are designed to ensure fairness, transparency, and responsible use of taxpayer money. That can mean writing and publishing a request for proposals (RFP), publicly soliciting bids, evaluating competing offers, and even allowing public comments that can all-too easily devolve into 17 hours of Pawnee-level discourse among stakeholders (real and imagined) about the relative merits of competing proposals.
Sourcewell is a government agency that basically does all that ahead of time , publishing RFPs, soliciting ,and evaluating bids against established criteria, then awarding contracts through a transparent, auditable process that makes competitively negotiated pricing available to more than 50,000 government, education and nonprofit organizations across the US and Canada.
In practice, that means your local government fleets can leverage Sourcewell to quickly adapt to pressing needs in a way that doesn’t bypass the bidding process (which would be illegal), but which effectively says, “we trust Sourcewell’s process.”
You can check out the full text of Sourcewell’s contract with Peterbilt, below, then let us know what you think of Pete’s efforts to electrify your local government fleet in the comments.

context_references.quote: That motorcycle still exists in small-scale production as the LiveWire One through H-D’s electric spinoff, but now LiveWire has wisened up to the real pathway to moving higher numbers of electric motorcycles with its S4 Honcho line .

source_document.body:
For years, the conventional wisdom surrounding electric motorcycles has been fairly straightforward: Build an electric motorcycle that’s just as good as a gasoline-powered motorcycle, make it affordable enough, and eventually riders will switch.
It’s essentially the same playbook that electric cars have followed. Make the electric version competitive enough, and eventually the market will move in that direction.
But I think we’ve been looking at electric motorcycles all wrong. Because the future of electric motorcycles isn’t necessarily about convincing today’s gasoline motorcycle riders to switch. It’s about the next generation of riders who won’t have any reason to start with gasoline in the first place.
And that’s a much bigger deal than it might sound. In fact, it’s the entire key to the puzzle. Because make no mistake, the future of motorcycling is electric. It just won’t happen the way most people think.
Advertisement - scroll for more content
Motorcycles aren’t cars
The problem with applying the electric car playbook to motorcycles is that motorcycles aren’t cars.
For most people, a car is a tool. It’s transportation. Sure, some drivers are deeply passionate about their cars, but they are a minority. The vast majority simply want something comfortable, reliable, affordable, and convenient to get them from point A to point B.
Motorcycles, especially in markets like the US and Europe, are different. In fact, it’s the complete opposite of the car situation. For a minority of Western riders, and especially American riders, a motorcycle is a tool. For the vast majority, it’s a passion. People generally buy motorcycles because they love motorcycles. And for many riders, that love is deeply intertwined with the gasoline engine itself.
The sound, the vibration, the shifting, the mechanical character. These aren’t necessarily flaws to be engineered away. They’re part of the experience for traditional riders.
You can show someone like that an electric motorcycle with better acceleration, lower maintenance costs, cheaper operating expenses, and the convenience of charging at home, and they still won’t want it.
Not because the electric motorcycle isn’t good enough, but because it isn’t what they love.
And that’s fine. There’s nothing wrong with loving gasoline motorcycles if that’s your thing. But it means that trying to convert those riders may be a losing battle, at least on any meaningful timeline.
Unfortunately though, it seems many years were wasted on that approach. Take Harley-Davidson, for example.
The brand started building its first electric motorcycle over a decade ago – commendable among all the other legacy motorcycle manufacturers that turned their noses up at the thought of going electric. When it was released in 2018 , the Harley-Davidson LiveWire received rave reviews, but it just didn’t sell well. For one, it was insanely expensive at $30,000. But the other major reason was that no matter how amazing it was, it wasn’t going to scratch that gasoline itch that most riders still had.
That motorcycle still exists in small-scale production as the LiveWire One through H-D’s electric spinoff, but now LiveWire has wisened up to the real pathway to moving higher numbers of electric motorcycles with its S4 Honcho line . And this brings us to how electric motorcycles will really replace their gasoline counterparts.
The next generation doesn’t have that baggage
Now consider what’s happening with younger riders today.
Millions of people are growing up riding electric bicycles, electric scooters, and increasingly powerful e-motos. For them, electric two-wheelers aren’t some strange new alternative to the real thing. They are the real thing.
They’ve grown accustomed to instant torque, quiet operation, and the simplicity of twisting a throttle and going. To these riders, a gasoline-powered motorcycle is laughably primitive. It’d be like me handing you a gasoline-powered drill or blender. Yeah, exactly. Now look who’s suddenly on team battery, eh?
So now we have a whole new generation of riders getting ready to come of age. And eventually, many of those riders are going to want something more.
Maybe they’ve spent years riding a 28 mph electric bike, or a 40 mph electric moto. Now they’re young adults, they want to ride on faster roads, and they want something capable of 70 or 80 mph that’s actually street legal. They’ve gone from a sixteen-year-old in a hoodie to a twenty-six-year-old in a collared shirt. Instead of getting to high school, now they’re getting to work. But they haven’t lost that desire to ride.
So what’s the natural next step?
An electric motorcycle.
It’s not because they’ve carefully compared electric and gasoline motorcycles and decided that electric is superior. It’s not because they’re trying to save the planet or reduce their maintenance costs. It’s simply because they grew up with electric two-wheelers as the norm.
It’s simply the next logical step in the type of riding they’ve already been doing for years.
Will a few of them transition over to gasoline-powered motorcycles? Sure. But for most, gasoline motorcycles will never even enter the equation.
Gasoline motorcycles won’t go out with a bang
Don’t get me wrong, we haven’t seen the last of gasoline motorcycles.
And I don’t even think electric motorcycles are going to suddenly outsell gasoline motorcycles because they become objectively better machines. At least not in the traditional recreational motorcycle markets we’re talking about here.
Instead, I think we’re going to see a somewhat more gradual generational transition.
Today’s gasoline motorcycle enthusiasts will largely keep riding gasoline motorcycles. They’ll keep buying them, maintaining them, and enjoying them for as long as they can.
But as those riders age out of motorcycling, the next generation won’t replace them with another generation of gasoline motorcycle buyers. In other words, gasoline motorcycles will die out with their riders.
Increasingly, those younger riders will have already entered the world of powered two-wheelers through electric bikes and e-motos. When they’re ready to move up, electric motorcycles will be waiting for them.
And over those next few years, the technology will only become better. The only remaining Achilles’ heel of electric motorcycles – their run time – will get better and better as battery technology improves and we move towards solid-state batteries.
Suddenly they’ll be on par with gasoline motorcycles for range and ‘fueling’ time, yet will beat those combustion bikes elsewhere. But at that point, “better” won’t even matter anymore as electrics will be the only comfortable option for the vast majority of new riders. Again, you wouldn’t buy a power drill that runs on a gasoline engine when you’ve seen how convenient and effective a lithium-ion power drill has been your whole life.
A Ryvid Anthem electric motorcycle that could serve as a stepping stone for someone accustomed to Sur Ron-style e-motos
Over time, the traditional gasoline motorcycle market will simply shrink as its existing customer base gets older, while electric motorcycles build an entirely new customer base alongside it.
And again, there will be exceptions in both directions. Some lifelong gasoline riders will enthusiastically embrace electric motorcycles, and some younger riders will still discover the appeal of combustion engines and running through the gears.
But the broader trend will be driven less by conversion and more by generational replacement.
That’s why electric motorcycles will eventually become the standard, even if they never manage to convince most of today’s gasoline motorcycle enthusiasts to switch.
Gasoline motorcycles won’t necessarily disappear because electric motorcycles finally beat them at their own game. They’ll fade because the next generation of riders will be playing a different game entirely.
In other words, and to paraphrase T. S. Eliot, gasoline motorcycles won’t go out with a bang, but with a whimper.
